catalog_quote: Tone is not contrastive, stress is predictable, and there are length contrasts. Stress is mainfested by increased amplitude, length, and pitch. Stress assignment is quantity-sensitive and feet are mainly bi-moraic trochees, with initial stress assignment being from right to left. There are, however, some words consisting of only a single CV syllable, for example te ‘ocean, salt, saltwater’, li ‘poison’, lu ‘armband’, mbi ‘molusc of the Trochus genus’, pa ‘Oblique preposition’, and to ‘Locative preposition’. So it is possible to have degenerate feet consisting of only a single syllable. Word stress is also assigned from right to left. Both vowels and syllable final consonants following a single vowel contribute to syllable weight. Length in vocoids is most accentuated when the word occurs at the end of a phonological phrase. The following constituents are extra-metrical, never receiving stress: 1. a final consonant or syllable following a long vowel 2. the Subject-indexing prefixes 3. the transitive suffixes at the end of words [p. 6] 4. the plural prefix –xa that occurs on inalienable nouns. The transitivity-altering prefixes pa ‘causative’, va (T) ~ wa (O) ‘reciprocal’, par ‘reciprocal’ and ma ‘detransitivizing’ seem to be inherently stressed, since they always receives secondary stress, regardless of the canonical shape of the verb root on which they occurs. [p. 7]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for mutu1242 and no existing stress statement, so this is the first statement for the language rather than a refinement of an earlier one: weight-sensitive, right-to-left bimoraic trochees with listed extrametrical morphemes. Authorship: the catalog and the SIL archive metadata credit Salme E. Bugenhagen, but the PDF title page reads 'Organised Phonology Data, By Robert Bugenhagen (Revised March 2009)' and 'Linguistic work done by: Robert and Salme Bugenhagen', and says the OPD reflects the Phonology Essentials approved by SIL consultants in 2001-2002 (i.e. the same analysis as Bugenhagen 2002 'Phonology of the Mutu-Tuam language').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and quantity-sensitive: bimoraic trochaic feet are built from the right edge of the word, and long vowels and closed syllables (a short vowel plus a coda consonant) count as heavy. Primary stress goes to the rightmost foot that is not extrametrical, so in practice the final syllable is stressed when it is heavy and eligible (e.g. [i'rɑ:β] 'go sailing', [tɑmɑ'mɑi] 'our father', [ipɑdu'du:ŋ] 'correct, teach') and the penult otherwise ([tin'ti:nɑ] 'big ones', ['ti.ti] 'walking stick', ['ɑ.tɛ] 'his liver'). Extrametrical, never stressed: a final consonant or syllable after a long vowel, subject-indexing prefixes (e.g. [ti'lɑ] 'they go'), word-final transitive suffixes, and the plural prefix -xa on inalienable nouns. Stress is realised by greater amplitude, length and pitch; vowel length is contrastive independently of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes. Trochaic feet are laid down right to left, so alternate feet leftward carry secondary stress; in addition, p. 7: 'The transitivity-altering prefixes pa ‘causative’, va (T) ~ wa (O) ‘reciprocal’, par ‘reciprocal’ and ma ‘detransitivizing’ seem to be inherently stressed, since they always receives secondary stress, regardless of the canonical shape of the verb root on which they occurs.'
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic CV words (te 'ocean', li 'poison', lu 'armband', mbi 'Trochus shell', pa 'oblique preposition', to 'locative preposition') form degenerate single-syllable feet; the four extrametrical classes listed in the quote; the 3PL accusative pronoun zi is marked '(unstressed)' on p. 3; vowel length is 'most accentuated when the word occurs at the end of a phonological phrase' (p. 6).
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD (work 0) covers the whole Saveeng / Mutu / Mutu-Tuam language (TUC) and names three dialects: Tuam (Tuam and Yaagha villages), Oov (Aramot, Mutu-Malau, Mandok, Aronai) and Malai; its stress statement is given for the language as a whole, with only the reciprocal prefix shown as dialect-specific (va in Tuam, wa in Oov). Work 1 is explicitly about the Tuam dialect ('Tuam is a dialect of the Oceanic Austronesian Saveeng language (aka Mutu-Tuam) spoken on Tuam and Umboi islands').

sources.note: Silent on stress. Only phonological remark is the orthography footnote on p. 455: 'In the orthography, nearly all symbols have their normal phonetic values. Gh represents a voiced velar fricative, v a bilabial fricative, and doubled vowels (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) represent long vowels.' Also states that Saveeng has three dialects: Tuam, Oov ('Mutu'), and Malai.
